content: The global food system currently occupies over one-third of the Earth's land surface and utilizes nearly 75% of freshwater resources for crop and livestock production. Despite this extensive use of resources, it fails to provide millions of people with healthy, safe, affordable, and sustainable diets. Poor dietary habits have become the leading cause of mortality worldwide, contributing to approximately 11 million premature adult deaths annually, as reported in the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017. Over half of these diet-related deaths and two-thirds of diet-related disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) are attributed to insufficient consumption of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, combined with excessive sodium intake. A new nutritional reality is emerging globally, characterized by the coexistence of undernutrition (including wasting, stunting, and micronutrient deficiencies) and overnutrition (manifesting as obesity and diet-related noncommunicable diseases) within the same populations, households, and even individuals. This double burden of malnutrition is particularly pronounced in lowand middle-income countries. This report aims to assist countries in transitioning toward healthier, more sustainable diets by integrating biodiversity into food-based interventions that support nutrition and health. It provides guidance for decision-makers in health, nutrition, and other sectors to recognize the critical role of biodiversity in food systems. This approach seeks to develop integrated interventions that promote diverse, sustainable diets, focus investments on comprehensive public health and nutrition projects, and enhance the resilience of food systems, health systems, and societies. These systems are increasingly threatened by ecological degradation, biodiversity loss, and climate change. Public health policies should adopt a health in all policies approach, ensuring that the impacts of biodiversity loss are reflected in strategies across various sectors. This approach maximizes shared health and environmental benefits by addressing upstream drivers of health hazards, including all forms of malnutrition. The United Nations Decade of Action on Nutrition (2016–2025), the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Paris Climate Agreement, and the emerging Global Biodiversity Framework provide a unique opportunity to develop coordinated, cross-sectoral actions. Biodiversity at all levels—genetic, species, and ecosystem—is foundational for food security, nutrition, and dietary quality. It provides essential variety in foods, nutrients, vitamins, minerals, and medicines, while supporting life-sustaining ecosystem services. Biodiversity is a core environmental determinant of health, influencing nutritional outcomes, livelihoods, gender equality, social equity, and other health determinants. Agrobiodiversity, in particular, offers a valuable resource for addressing malnutrition by providing dietary energy, macronutrients, micronutrients, and bioactive compounds. Soil biodiversity plays a crucial role in filtering water and pollutants, enhancing crop yield and nutrient content, reducing pests and diseases, and protecting against foodborne, waterborne, and soilborne illnesses. Agroecological practices, such as soil mulching and cover crop cultivation, improve soil quality, reduce food loss and waste, and enhance food safety. However, the narrowing diversity of crops and breeds in managed agroecosystems, along with reduced access to sustainably harvested wild species, has limited the availability of healthy and nutritious diets for many vulnerable communities. Millions of people rely on wild foods for protein, micronutrients, food security, and medicinal plants. Sustainable harvesting and use of wild species safeguard scientific, traditional, and ethnobiological knowledge while preserving ecosystems. Biodiversity can play a more prominent role in planning for nutritional outcomes through practices like sustainable agroforestry, which supports the production of nutritious fruits and plant products, sustains livelihoods, and increases product diversity in markets. Achieving these goals requires bold, coordinated, and multisectoral action involving nutrition, agriculture, health, biodiversity conservation, trade, education, water supply, sanitation, and social protection. Cross-cutting issues such as gender equality, governance, and state fragility must also be addressed. Recognizing the global challenge of climate change is essential, as is harnessing the potential of local agrobiodiversity and shifting consumption patterns away from animal-sourced products in high meat consumption societies toward less emission-intensive sources. Transformative changes can be achieved through approaches like agroforestry, wetland and mangrove restoration, and sustainable land management practices. These strategies enhance the sustainability of food production systems, address public health risks, and align policy decisions with global commitments. Traditional food systems, particularly those of Indigenous Peoples, are diverse and represent critical repositories of knowledge for healthy, resilient diets with minimal environmental impact. Strengthening these systems can improve diets, reverse negative health outcomes, support community cohesion, and preserve cultural values and identities. Policy coherence must be ensured through institutional and cross-sectoral collaboration and good governance. The Second International Conference on Nutrition (ICN2) Framework for Action provides policy options to make food systems more sustainable and supportive of diverse, healthy diets. Shared principles of sustainability in promoting healthy diets are essential. This guidance outlines six core building blocks for mainstreaming biodiversity for nutrition and health: cross-sectoral knowledge development, enabling environments, integration of biodiversity into research and policy, conservation and wider use of biodiversity, education and awareness-raising, and monitoring and evaluation. These building blocks are complementary and iterative, adapting to new knowledge, evolving structures, and changing environmental, socioeconomic, and health conditions. Examples of targeted measures include promoting indigenous crop varieties, adopting integrated pest management, improving soil health management, supporting local food production and consumption, restoring vegetation in catchments, sustainably managing fish habitats, improving post-harvest methods, and making healthy local foods accessible to school-aged children. Education on the nutritional value of locally sourced foods and supporting smallholder farmers in producing biodiverse foods linked to school feeding programs are also critical. Success indicators must go beyond agricultural performance to include the benefits of healthy, sustainable diets, reduced health risks, and the nutritional, environmental, and socioeconomic advantages of locally produced foods. These indicators should support evidence-based policy decisions that promote co-benefits and strengthen social and ecological resilience to external shocks, including climate shocks and disasters. The opportunity to mainstream biodiversity for healthy and sustainable diets is unprecedented. The scientific evidence is robust, and the urgency to transform the global food system has never been greater.
